paragraphs.text: Parcel point at Corner News — how collection works. When a delivery cannot be left at your address, the driver brings it here and you receive a message with a six-digit code. Parcels are held for seven days, counted from the morning after they arrive, and are returned to the sender on the eighth. We are open from 7 am to 8 pm on weekdays, 8 am to 6 pm on Saturdays and 9 am to 1 pm on Sundays.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Bring the code and one form of identification with your name on it; a bank card is accepted, a photograph of a document on a telephone is not. Somebody else may collect for you if they have the code and their own identification, and if you have replied to the message with their name. We cannot hand over a parcel to a person under sixteen, and parcels marked as containing alcohol are released only to someone who looks over twenty-five or can show a date of birth.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: There is no charge for collection. Returns may also be left here if the label is already printed and attached; we do not print labels and cannot accept a parcel with a code on a screen. Fragile items are kept behind the counter, but we do not insure anything and cannot be held responsible for damage that happened before the parcel reached us. If your parcel is not here when the message says it should be, wait until the end of the day before reporting it, as vans sometimes arrive late.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Bramble Farm shop — what we sell and how to order. The shop is open Wednesday to Sunday, 9 am to 5 pm, and is closed on Monday and Tuesday while the fields are picked. We sell our own vegetables and fruit, eggs from the farm, bread baked here on Thursdays and Saturdays, and cheese, honey and juice from farms within twenty miles. Everything is priced by weight at the counter; we do not sell packs of mixed vegetables at a fixed price.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Boxes are made up to order for collection on Fridays. A small box feeds one or two people and costs £14, a large box feeds four and costs £24, and both contain whatever is ready that week rather than a fixed list; you may exclude up to three items you do not eat. Order by Wednesday evening through the form on our page or by leaving a note at the counter. Payment is taken when you collect, by card or in cash.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: We deliver on Fridays to villages within eight miles for £3, free on orders over £35. Deliveries are left in a safe place agreed when you order, and we send a message when the driver leaves the farm. Boxes not collected by 5 pm on Friday are held in the cold room until Saturday morning and are then given to the community fridge. Please return the crates: we reuse them, and a lost crate costs us more than the box it carried.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: C
texts.title: Working nights: what the rota guarantees

paragraphs.text: Working nights: what the rota guarantees. A night shift runs from 10 pm to 6 am and counts as eight hours for pay, with a thirty-minute paid break taken away from the machines. No employee works more than four night shifts in a row, and a run of four is followed by at least two days off before the next run begins. The rota is published four weeks ahead and changes to it within a week of the shift need the agreement of the person affected.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Night workers are entitled to a health assessment before starting and once a year afterwards. It is short, it is arranged in working time, and it is confidential: the company is told whether you are fit for night work and nothing else. If the assessment recommends a move to day shifts, the company must offer a day post at the same grade where one exists, and where none exists the case goes to the site manager rather than being closed.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Pay for nights is the basic rate plus a supplement of twenty per cent, and the supplement is paid on the hours actually worked at night rather than on the whole shift when a shift crosses midnight in the other direction. Overtime on a night shift is paid at the same supplement; it is never offered to somebody who has already worked four nights in a row, and a supervisor who arranges that is in breach of the rota rules rather than being helpful.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Practical arrangements matter more than the leaflets suggest. Hot food is available from the canteen at 1 am, the rest room has a sofa and no fixed lighting, and transport is provided for anybody finishing at 6 am who cannot get home before the first bus. Nobody is asked to drive a works vehicle after a fourth consecutive night. If you are struggling with sleep, tell your supervisor before it becomes a safety matter; this is treated as an ordinary conversation and is not recorded on your file.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Keys, passes and building security. Every employee is issued a pass that opens the doors their role requires and no others, and access is reviewed when a role changes rather than when somebody remembers. The pass is personal: lending it is a disciplinary matter, not because the company distrusts its staff but because the record of who was in the building has to mean something after an incident.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Report a lost pass the same day, by telephone if it is outside office hours. The old pass is cancelled within the hour and a replacement is issued at the reception desk the next working day; the first replacement in a year is free and further ones cost £15. A pass that is found after being reported cannot be reactivated and must be handed in, because a cancelled pass that starts working again is exactly the hole the system is designed to prevent.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Visitors sign in at reception, wear a badge and are accompanied at all times by the person they are visiting; contractors sign a separate book and are given a pass that expires at the end of the day. Do not hold a door open for somebody you do not recognise, however uncomfortable that feels: the phrase we use is that the door is not being rude to them, and reception will let anybody in who should be in.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Two rules apply after hours. Anybody working alone in the building after 8 pm signs the late book and tells the security desk when they leave, so that a car left in the car park at midnight is never a mystery. And the last person out of a floor checks that the windows are shut and the doors closed behind them, including the ones they did not open; this sounds like a small matter and is the single thing most often missed in the weekly check.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A weather forecast is the most widely used scientific product in the world, and almost nobody notices how much better it has become. A five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a two-day forecast was forty years ago, and the improvement has been steady rather than sudden, arriving in increments that were individually too small to be newsworthy. The public memory of forecasting is formed by the failures, which is unfair and is also the reason the profession is so careful with its language.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Modern forecasting rests on an idea that is a century old and was useless when it was proposed. The atmosphere obeys equations, so given the state of the air now, the state tomorrow can in principle be calculated; the first person to try it by hand produced a forecast that took months to compute and was badly wrong. The idea needed three things that arrived later: enough observations to describe the starting state, a machine fast enough to do the arithmetic, and a way of handling the fact that small errors in the starting state grow.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Observations are the least glamorous of the three and matter most. Surface stations, balloons, aircraft, ships and buoys contribute, but the transformation came from satellites, which now supply the great majority of the data that enters a model. What a satellite measures is not temperature or wind directly but radiation at particular wavelengths, from which the state of the atmosphere is inferred, and the calculation that turns one into the other is itself a substantial piece of science.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The growth of small errors is the reason forecasts have a horizon at all. Two starting states that differ by less than the accuracy of any instrument will produce forecasts that diverge, slowly at first and then completely, and no improvement in computing removes this; it is a property of the atmosphere rather than of the method. The practical response is to run the model many times from slightly different starting points and to treat the spread of the results as the forecast, which is why a modern forecast is a probability rather than a statement.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Getting the public to use probabilities has proved harder than producing them. A forecast of a thirty per cent chance of rain is frequently read as a promise that it will not rain, and a day on which it rains is then recorded as a failure; the same figure presented as three days in ten is understood better. Broadcasters differ in how much of this they attempt, and the research suggests that people handle probability well when it is expressed in a form they can count.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The value of the improvement is easiest to see where the weather is dangerous. Warnings of storms and floods that arrive a day earlier change what can be done: a hospital can move patients, a port can secure its cranes, a farmer can bring in a harvest, and a city can position its pumps. Studies of storm warnings in several countries find that the economic return on the whole forecasting system is dominated by a handful of such events, and that the ordinary daily forecast is close to free by comparison.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Two changes are under way that will make the next twenty years look different. Models that learn from the archive of past weather rather than solving the equations directly have, in the past few years, matched and in some measures beaten the traditional models at a fraction of the computing cost, which nobody in the field expected so soon. And forecasts at the scale of a city, which require resolving individual storms, are becoming possible, which matters because a flood happens in one district and not in another.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What has not changed is the weakest link. A forecast is only as useful as the warning that reaches somebody who can act on it, and the gap between a good forecast and a good outcome is filled by sirens, messages, local officials and habits built by practice. Several countries with excellent forecasting have poor warning systems, and several with modest forecasting have excellent ones; the second group loses fewer people. That is an uncomfortable finding for a science that measures itself in accuracy.
paragraphs.label: H
